notes.h: Rate of photosynthesis and limiting factors
notes.b: Before measuring anything, you need to know what "rate" means and which conditions can speed photosynthesis up or hold it back. This theory is what every hypothesis in the investigation rests on.
points: The rate of photosynthesis is the amount of product made, or reactant used, per unit time. It is usually measured as the rate of oxygen production, in bubbles per minute or cm³ of gas per minute, but it can also be measured as the rate of CO₂ uptake.
Oxygen is a good thing to measure because it is a product: it comes from the splitting of water in the light-dependent stage (the first stage, which needs light).

Light intensity: light supplies the energy for the light-dependent stage, so more light means more ATP (the cell's energy carrier) and hydrogen are made per minute and the rate rises, until another factor holds it back.
Carbon dioxide concentration: CO₂ is the raw material of the light-independent stage (the second stage, which builds glucose), so more CO₂ raises the rate, until another factor holds it back.

Temperature: the light-independent stage is controlled by enzymes. Raising the temperature increases the rate, because molecules move faster and collide more often with the enzymes' active sites (the part of the enzyme where the reaction happens), up to an optimum.
Above the optimum the rate falls quickly, because the enzymes are denatured (their shape is permanently changed, so they stop working). There is more on this in Enzymes as catalysts.

A limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply, which holds back the rate of a process even when the other factors are increased. At any moment the rate is limited by whichever of light intensity, CO₂ concentration or temperature is furthest from its best value.
Raising a limiting factor increases the rate. Raising a factor that is not limiting has no effect, because something else is still holding the rate back.
notes.tip: If asked to explain a limiting factor, say it is the factor in shortest supply and that raising it raises the rate, while raising a factor that is not limiting does nothing. Remember that only high temperatures denature enzymes: at low temperatures the rate is low because molecules move slowly.

notes.b: The bubbles you count are not the whole story. A plant is also respiring, and respiration uses oxygen, so what you measure is a net result.
points: A plant respires all the time, using some of the oxygen it makes, so the oxygen given off is photosynthesis minus respiration. This is called the net (apparent) rate.
In very dim light the two processes are equal and no oxygen is given off, because all the oxygen made is used up. This is the compensation point.
In darkness there is no photosynthesis, so the plant takes in oxygen for respiration.

notes.h: Investigation planning: aim, hypotheses and choice of plant
notes.b: A good investigation changes one thing and measures one thing. Planning starts with a clear aim, a prediction for each factor, and a plant that lets you see the result.
points: Aim: to investigate the effect of light intensity (or CO₂ concentration, or temperature) on the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed. Write one investigation per factor, changing only that factor, so you know which one caused any change.

Hypothesis for light: as light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until it levels off. This rests on the theory that light drives the light-dependent stage until something else becomes limiting.
Hypothesis for CO₂: as CO₂ concentration increases, the rate increases until it levels off. This rests on CO₂ being the raw material of the light-independent stage.
Hypothesis for temperature: the rate increases with temperature up to an optimum and then decreases, because the enzymes of the light-independent stage work faster until they are denatured.

Elodea (Canadian pondweed) is the standard school plant. It is aquatic, so the oxygen it gives off appears as visible bubbles from the cut stem, which can be counted or collected. It is also easy to obtain, grows quickly and photosynthesises rapidly.

notes.h: Investigation planning: variables, control and equipment
notes.b: Next you decide what to change, what to measure and what to hold steady, and gather the apparatus. The variables below are for the light-intensity investigation.
points: The independent variable (the one you change) is light intensity, set by the lamp's distance from the plant or measured with a light meter in lux.
The dependent variable (the one you measure) is the rate of oxygen production, as bubbles per minute or cm³ of gas per minute.

Controlled variables (kept the same, so they cannot affect the result): temperature (water bath), CO₂ concentration (same sodium hydrogencarbonate concentration), the same pondweed (species, length, leaves), the same lamp and bulb, the adjustment time and the counting period.
For the other factors, swap the independent variable for CO₂ concentration or temperature, and keep light intensity constant.

Control: an identical set-up kept in darkness (lamp off, tube covered with foil), or a tube with no plant, gives no bubbles. This shows that the bubbles come from photosynthesis by the plant in the light, not from gas leaving the solution.

Equipment: fresh Elodea, scalpel or scissors, boiling tube or test tube, paper clip to weigh the pondweed down, beaker as a water bath (or an electric water bath), thermometer, bench lamp (an LED bulb gives out less heat), metre stick, stopwatch, and a light meter (optional).
Chemicals: sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO₃) powder, or solutions of known concentration, which supplies the plant with CO₂, in water that has been boiled and cooled.
For measuring volume: a funnel and graduated tube, or a capillary tube attached to a syringe, called a photosynthometer. A glowing splint is optional, for testing the gas.

notes.b: This basic set-up is used for all three investigations. Only the factor you change differs, so learn it once and adapt it.
points: 1. Fill a boiling tube with water containing a set concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate. It dissolves to supply CO₂ to the plant, so that CO₂ is not limiting (except in the carbon dioxide investigation).
2. Cut a healthy shoot of pondweed about 5 to 8 cm long, cutting the stem cleanly and slantwise under water.
3. Place it in the tube upside down, with the cut end at the top, weighed down with a paper clip.
4. Stand the tube in a beaker of water at a constant temperature, for example 25 °C, checked with a thermometer, so the temperature stays steady.
5. Carry out the investigation in a darkened room, so that the lamp is the only light source.

Counting: let the plant adjust to each new condition for about 5 minutes, then count the bubbles leaving the cut end in one minute. Repeat the count three times at each setting and calculate the mean.

Collecting (more accurate): place an inverted funnel over the pondweed in a beaker, with a water-filled graduated tube over its stem, and record the gas collected in a set time, for example 5 minutes. Alternatively, draw the gas up a capillary tube with a syringe and measure the bubble's length.

Volume per unit time is more accurate than counting, because bubbles vary in size. Optional gas test: it relights a glowing splint, so it is rich in oxygen, but not pure oxygen, since dissolved nitrogen and carbon dioxide also come out.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to name the plant and give a reason for using it, to state how the rate was measured, and to say how temperature was kept constant (a water bath checked with a thermometer).

notes.b: Here the independent variable is light intensity, which you change by moving the lamp. The challenge is changing the light without also changing the temperature.
points: 1. Set up as in the basic set-up.
2. Place the lamp 10 cm from the pondweed, measured with a metre stick from the bulb to the plant.
3. Allow 5 minutes to adjust, then count the bubbles per minute three times.
4. Move the lamp to 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm, and repeat.
5. Check the water temperature at each distance and keep it constant, by adding cold or warm water to the bath.

A lamp close to the plant also heats it, which would change two variables at once. Use an LED bulb, or place a beaker or flat-sided tank of water between the lamp and the plant as a heat shield, and check the thermometer.

Moving the lamp further away lowers the light intensity as the inverse square of the distance (light intensity ∝ 1/d²): doubling the distance gives a quarter of the light intensity. It does not fall in simple proportion.
So plot the rate against 1/d² to show the relationship with light intensity, or measure the light intensity at each position with a light meter.
notes.tip: Students often forget the heating effect of the lamp, so say how you keep temperature constant. Don't plot rate against distance and call it light intensity: use 1/d² or a light meter.

notes.b: Here the independent variable is CO₂ concentration, which you change by using sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions of different strengths. Light and temperature are held constant.
points: 1. Make up a series of sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions of increasing concentration, for example 0%, 0.25%, 0.5%, 0.75% and 1%, using water that has been boiled and cooled. Boiling removes dissolved CO₂, so the 0% tube has very little.
2. Keep the lamp at a fixed distance close to the plant, for example 10 cm, and keep the temperature constant, so that CO₂ is the only thing that changes.
3. Place the same pondweed in each solution in turn, allow 5 minutes to adjust, and count the bubbles per minute three times.
4. Calculate the mean for each concentration.
notes.tip: Sodium hydrogencarbonate is the source of CO₂ (through hydrogencarbonate ions). It is not a nutrient or a source of oxygen, and the bubbles are mostly oxygen, not carbon dioxide.

notes.b: Here the independent variable is temperature, changed with water baths. Light and CO₂ are held constant.
points: 1. Set up as in the basic set-up, with a fixed lamp distance and a fixed sodium hydrogencarbonate concentration.
2. Place the tube in a water bath at a range of temperatures, for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C, using ice or warm water or electric water baths, and check each with a thermometer.
3. Let the tube reach the bath temperature, about 5 minutes, then count the bubbles per minute three times.
4. If the first pondweed stops producing bubbles, use a fresh piece for the higher temperatures, and note that you have done so.
Warm water holds less dissolved gas, so some bubbles at high temperatures can come from gas leaving the solution. The darkness control at each temperature checks this.

notes.b: This investigation mixes electricity, water, heat and sharp tools, so each hazard needs its own precaution.
points: Electricity and water: keep the lamp, its cable and plug away from the water bath, dry your hands before touching switches, and do not move a lamp while it is on and hot.
Lamp bulbs, other than LEDs, get very hot and can burn, so let them cool before moving them.
Take care with the scalpel: cut on a tile, away from the body. Take care with hot water baths and glassware.
Wash your hands after handling pondweed and pond water.

Elodea canadensis is a non-native invasive species (one that spreads and harms native wildlife) in Ireland. Never put leftover pondweed or its water into ponds, lakes, rivers or drains; dispose of it in compost or general waste.

notes.b: The results table and graph turn counts into a relationship you can explain. For each factor the shape of the graph tells you what is limiting the rate.
points: Record the primary data (the results you collect yourself) in a table: the independent variable (distance in cm and 1/d², concentration in %, or temperature in °C), the three counts and the mean number of bubbles per minute.
Plot the mean rate on the y-axis against the independent variable on the x-axis, with units, and join the points with a smooth curve or straight lines.

Light intensity: as the lamp moves closer, the rate increases, so it falls as distance increases. At high intensity the curve levels off in a plateau, because another factor, CO₂ concentration or temperature, has become limiting.
CO₂ concentration: the rate increases with CO₂ concentration and then levels off, because light intensity or temperature becomes limiting. At 0% (boiled water) there are few or no bubbles.

Temperature: the rate rises up to an optimum, then falls steeply above it, as the enzymes of the light-independent stage are denatured. Bubbling may stop at the highest temperatures. The curve is not symmetrical: the fall is steeper than the rise.
Conclusion: state the relationship shown by the primary data and whether it supports the hypothesis. On the levelling-off part of the graph, name the factor that is now limiting.
notes.tip: A plateau means another factor is limiting, not that the plant is full or that enzymes are denatured. Denaturation explains only the fall at high temperature.

notes.b: Examiners often ask you to draw the apparatus or sketch the expected graphs. Learn the labels for each.
points: Diagram: the set-up. Labels: lamp, metre stick, heat shield, beaker water bath, thermometer, boiling tube of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, upside-down pondweed with bubbles at the cut end (or the funnel and graduated collecting tube).

Diagram: two sketch graphs. (a) Rate against light intensity, rising then levelling off, plus a higher curve labelled higher CO₂ concentration; label the rise light limiting and the plateau CO₂ or temperature limiting. (b) Rate against temperature, rising to an optimum then falling steeply.
notes.tip: For a graph of rate against light intensity or CO₂ concentration, sketch and label it over a wide range and explain the shape: it rises, then levels off as another factor becomes limiting.

notes.b: Your own results are only one source. You can also use other people's data to support a conclusion, and apply the idea of limiting factors to growing crops.
points: Secondary data are results collected by others: other groups' class results, textbook or published graphs, or data-logger results from an oxygen or CO₂ sensor. Pooling class results increases the sample size and checks reproducibility (whether others get the same result).

Interpreting a graph of rate against light intensity at two CO₂ concentrations (or two temperatures): where the two curves overlap, light is the limiting factor, because raising CO₂ makes no difference.
Where the two curves separate and each levels off, CO₂ (or temperature) is limiting, because raising it raises the plateau.

Applying limiting factors: commercial glasshouse growers raise the yield of crops such as tomatoes and lettuce by supplying extra light (artificial lighting), heat and CO₂. Burning paraffin or propane gives both heat and CO₂, or CO₂ gas can be added.
Each factor is kept just high enough that it is not limiting. Raising a factor that is not limiting wastes fuel and money and adds to emissions.
notes.tip: If asked how limiting factors apply to greenhouse growing, name the factors a grower can supply (light, heat, CO₂) and say each is raised only while it is limiting.

notes.b: No school investigation is perfect. Knowing where the errors come from tells you how to reduce them.
points: Bubbles vary in size and can be missed or merge when the rate is fast, so counting is imprecise. Collecting the volume of gas is more accurate.
Other light in the room, such as daylight or other groups' lamps, changes the light intensity, so work in a darkened room.
Temperature can drift, especially with a hot bulb close to the plant, so check it and adjust it.
The gas is not pure oxygen, and some oxygen dissolves in the water instead of forming bubbles, so the bubbles underestimate the true rate. The measured rate is also a net rate, after respiration.
The carbon dioxide from sodium hydrogencarbonate is used up over time, and the plant's response may change, so use fresh solution, a fresh plant for each run if needed, and repeat the whole series.
Allowing too little time to adjust after each change gives rates that still reflect the previous setting.
Repeat each reading at least three times and calculate a mean, so a single odd count has less effect. Compare your results with other groups' results.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of product made, or reactant used, per unit time; often measured as the rate of oxygen production.
The factor in shortest supply, which holds back the rate of a process even when the other factors are increased.
The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration, so no net gas exchange occurs.
The temperature at which enzyme-controlled reactions proceed fastest; above it the enzymes are denatured and the rate falls.
Light intensity falls as the inverse square of the distance from the source, so doubling the distance gives a quarter of the intensity.
Results collected by others, such as other groups' results, textbook graphs or data-logger results, used to support conclusions.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a limiting factor, and name two factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.model: A limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply, which holds back the rate of a process even when the other factors are increased. Raising a limiting factor increases the rate, while raising a factor that is not limiting has no effect. Two factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis are light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration; temperature can also be limiting.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis. Include how you would vary light intensity, measure the rate and keep two other factors constant.
questions.model: Use a fresh shoot of pondweed (Elodea), cut slantwise under water and placed upside down in a boiling tube of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, which supplies carbon dioxide so that it is not limiting. Weigh the shoot down with a paper clip and keep the tube in a darkened room, with a lamp as the only light source. Vary light intensity by moving the lamp to distances such as 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm from the plant, measured with a metre stick; light intensity falls as the inverse square of the distance, so doubling the distance gives a quarter of the intensity, or measure intensity with a light meter. Allow about 5 minutes to adjust at each distance, then count the bubbles of oxygen leaving the cut end in one minute, repeat three times and calculate the mean. Measure rate as the mean number of bubbles per minute. Keep temperature constant by standing the tube in a water bath checked with a thermometer, and use an LED bulb or a heat shield to stop the lamp heating the water. Keep the carbon dioxide concentration constant by using the same sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, and use the same piece of pondweed for each run. Include a control in darkness, which gives no bubbles, to show that the bubbles come from photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Sketch a graph of the expected results of an investigation into the effect of carbon dioxide concentration on the rate of photosynthesis, and explain its shape. Suggest how a glasshouse grower could use this information.
questions.model: Plot rate of photosynthesis on the y-axis against carbon dioxide concentration on the x-axis. The line rises as the concentration increases, then levels off at a plateau. The rise occurs because carbon dioxide is the raw material of the light-independent stage, so more of it raises the rate. The plateau occurs because another factor, light intensity or temperature, has become limiting, so raising carbon dioxide further makes no difference. A glasshouse grower can use this to supply carbon dioxide only up to the level where it stops being limiting, for example by burning paraffin or propane or adding CO₂ gas, and not beyond it, since extra carbon dioxide beyond that point wastes money and adds to emissions.
